opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. There are a few I take seriously, and they interact.

**Compute scaling hitting economic limits.** A lot of recent progress has come from pouring more compute into training runs, and that compute has been growing several times over each year. That can't continue indefinitely on the current trajectory. At some point you're talking about training runs that cost a meaningful fraction of the GDP of major countries, or that need dedicated power plants, fabs, and chip supply chains that take years to build. If companies aren't seeing enough revenue to justify the next order of magnitude, investment could plateau. Around the end of this decade we'll start running into these limits pretty hard. So in my mind there's a "now or never-ish" dynamic: either we get to something transformative while compute is still scaling fast, or progress slows considerably and timelines stretch out a lot.

**Data.** We've used up a large fraction of the high-quality human text on the internet. I think this is less of a bottleneck than people sometimes assume, because there are workarounds like synthetic data, reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks, multimodal data, and learning from interaction with environments. But it's a real constraint, and it shapes *what kind* of progress we get.

**Long-horizon agency.** This is the one I think about most. Models are getting very good at short tasks, but the key question is whether they can reliably do tasks that take a human days or weeks: staying on track, noticing and fixing their own mistakes, managing a big project. The trend lines there look pretty steep, with the length of tasks AIs can handle doubling on a timescale of months. But it's possible we hit a wall where getting from "hours" to "weeks" requires some qualitatively new insight that doesn't come from just scaling RL on agentic tasks. If that's true, it could add years.

**Things that are hard to measure.** A lot of what matters for automating AI research itself is research taste: choosing which experiments to run and interpreting ambiguous results. That's harder to train for, because you can't easily generate a reward signal for it. If progress on the easily checkable stuff races ahead while taste lags, the intelligence-explosion dynamics could be slower than I'd otherwise expect.

**Things I take less seriously.** Regulation slowing things down substantially seems unlikely to me given current political dynamics, though I'd personally like more of it. And I don't put much weight on claims that deep learning is fundamentally incapable of reasoning; that view has made a lot of failed predictions.

So overall, I think these bottlenecks are why my median is a few years out rather than next year, and why there's a fat tail stretching into the 2030s and beyond. But none of them seem decisive enough to make me comfortable. The default trajectory still looks like it gets somewhere very dramatic quite soon.

r001.rationale: The response says claims that deep learning cannot reason have made failed predictions, but it does not cite the trend’s emergence within the existing paradigm as the reason to doubt that missing capabilities will slow progress.

r002.rationale: It says companies may not see enough revenue to justify the next order of magnitude of compute investment, causing investment to plateau.

r003.rationale: It discusses compute growth eventually plateauing or becoming constrained, but does not argue that progress can slow while inputs keep growing exponentially at a lower rate.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I want to be clear up front that I do take these seriously — my forecasts have fairly wide error bars, and a lot of the probability mass on the slower side comes from exactly these kinds of bottlenecks. Let me go through the ones I think matter most.

The first and probably the biggest is compute. The trend over the last several years has been training runs getting something like four to five times bigger every year, and that's been driven by companies pouring enormous amounts of money into chips and data centers. That can't continue indefinitely at that rate. At some point you run into the actual physical supply of chips, the fabs, the energy — people are talking about gigawatt-scale data centers, and getting the power for those is a genuine engineering and political problem. So I expect the compute growth rate to slow at some point, and the question is just whether that happens before or after you get to systems that can substantially automate AI research. If it happens before, then things could look a lot more gradual than in our scenarios.

Related to that is the money. These companies are spending tens of billions, heading toward hundreds of billions, and so far investors are willing to fund it because they expect enormous returns. But if the revenue doesn't materialize fast enough — if the products are useful but not that useful — you could get a pullback. An AI winter, or at least an AI autumn. I think that's a real possibility, and it's one I probably underweighted a couple of years ago.

The second big category is data. We've basically used up the high-quality text on the internet. The labs are compensating with synthetic data and with reinforcement learning on tasks where you can verify the answer — math, code, things like that. That's working well in those domains, but it's an open question how far it generalizes. If it turns out that getting good at verifiable tasks doesn't transfer to the messy, long-horizon, agentic stuff that actually matters for automating research, then you could see progress that looks impressive on benchmarks but stalls out in terms of real-world capability. I think this is one of the more important cruxes, honestly.

The third thing — and this is maybe more of an algorithmic bottleneck than a resource bottleneck — is the question of whether current approaches can get to the kind of agency and long-horizon coherence you need. Right now these systems are great at tasks that take a human a few minutes or maybe an hour or two. The trend in task length has been doubling every several months, which is fast. But maybe there's some wall there. Maybe continual learning, or something about how humans accumulate experience on the job, turns out to be a hard problem that doesn't fall just from scaling. I don't think that's the most likely outcome, but I give it real weight.

And then I'd add a couple of things that aren't about the technology at all. One is regulation or political backlash — if there's a major incident, or just a shift in public mood, governments could slow things down significantly. I don't currently expect that to happen in time to matter much, but I could be wrong. The other is more mundane: organizational dysfunction. Even if the technology is there, turning it into an intelligence explosion requires the labs to actually deploy it internally, trust it, restructure their workflows around it. That could be slower and messier than the clean version in a model.

So if I had to summarize: compute and funding constraints are the most likely reason the trend bends, data and generalization are the most important technical uncertainty, and then there's a tail of things — algorithmic walls, political shocks — that could each independently slow things down. Put all that together and I'd say it's quite plausible that we're talking about the 2030s rather than the late 2020s. But I'd also say the opposite tail is real, and I don't think any of these bottlenecks are so solid that I'd want to bet the house on them.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses possible limits of current approaches and does not argue that progress within the existing paradigm is a reason to doubt missing capabilities will slow it.

r002.rationale: It says companies are spending tens of billions and may pull back if returns do not materialize, linking finite funding to a possible slowdown in compute growth.

r003.rationale: It says compute growth may slow and progress may become more gradual, even before compute stops growing; this communicates that a lower growth rate can bend the trend.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between things that could slow down scaling and things that could mean scaling doesn’t translate into the capabilities we care about.

On the first, compute isn’t something you can expand indefinitely without running into constraints. You need chips, electricity, data centres, and the money to pay for all of that. If the economic returns disappoint, companies might become less willing to fund the next big jump. Those seem like real reasons progress could slow down, even if the underlying methods keep working.

Data is another possibility. You can’t just assume there will always be more high-quality human-generated text available. You can try to substitute synthetic data or learning from interaction with an environment, but then the question is how well those approaches work. Generating more examples isn’t necessarily the same as generating more useful information.

The bottleneck I’d be particularly interested in is whether systems can reliably do long, complicated tasks. Being impressive in a short interaction is different from carrying out a research project where you have to make thousands of decisions, notice when you’re wrong, and recover. It’s possible that improving that reliability requires something we don’t yet know how to do.

So I take those possibilities seriously. But I’d be cautious about moving from ‘there’s a potential bottleneck here’ to ‘therefore we can count on a long delay.’ A bottleneck can be real and still turn out to be something people work around.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between bottlenecks to building more capable models and bottlenecks to turning those capabilities into economic impact. You could have very rapid progress on the first and much slower progress on the second.

On the first, compute is a real constraint. You need chips, power, data centres, and the money to pay for all of that. If the next step requires a much bigger training run, you can’t necessarily make that happen immediately. Eventually, companies might also find that the improvements aren’t worth the cost.

Data is another possibility. You can’t just assume that generating more synthetic data will solve the problem, because you need some way of distinguishing good outputs from bad ones. That’s relatively straightforward in domains where you can check an answer, but harder elsewhere. So I take seriously the possibility that progress becomes uneven: very fast in some areas and much slower in others.

And then there’s the possibility that the current methods simply stop delivering the improvements we expect. I don’t think we should rule that out. Getting better at the tasks we currently measure might not translate into being able to carry out a complicated project reliably over weeks or months.

But the question is whether these things cause a temporary delay or a sustained slowdown. If AI systems become useful enough at doing AI research, they could help work around several of those bottlenecks. So naming a constraint isn’t, by itself, enough to establish that progress will slow down for very long.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses compute, data, and methods as possible bottlenecks, but does not argue that progress within the existing paradigm makes missing capabilities beyond it less likely to slow the trend.

r002.rationale: It mentions money as a cost and says improvements may not be worth that cost, but does not identify companies’ finite financial resources as a constraint that will eventually slow compute growth for training runs.
